segments.narration: Eleven churches in Ethiopia were carved downward out of bedrock. Lalibela, up in the Amhara highlands. No blocks, no mortar, no scaffolding.
Crews cut trenches straight down into volcanic rock, then hollowed out the block they had left standing in the middle. Roof first. Floor last.
Four of them stand completely free of the mountain. Tunnels run between the groups. One, Bete Giyorgis, is a giant cross sunk into the ground.
Tradition gives all of it to one king, Gebre Meskel Lalibela, around 1200, and says the eleven took twenty-four years. The rock disagrees.
Archaeologist David Phillipson dated the earliest cuttings to the seventh or eighth century. Four or five building phases, five hundred years of work, and one king's name on the whole thing.

verdicts.claim: The eleven rock-hewn churches at Lalibela in Amhara, Ethiopia, were carved downward out of living rock rather than built up from blocks.
verdicts.note: 80% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: Workers cut trenches around the structures with hammers and chisels in scoriaceous basalt, carving top-down so the lowest part is cut last.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia names the hammers, chisels and scoriaceous basalt and the trenches; the Met states the top-down approach 'leaves the most recently hewn element at the bottom'.

verdicts.claim: Four of the eleven are free-standing monoliths, tunnels link the church groups, and Biete Giorgis is cruciform in plan.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia gives the four monoliths, the linking tunnels and Biete Giorgis as cruciform and independent. No source checked gives its dimensions, so the narration gives none.

verdicts.claim: Tradition attributes the churches to King Gebre Meskel Lalibela, reigning about 1181 to 1221, and holds that the eleven took twenty-four years.
verdicts.note: 73% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Archaeologist David Phillipson dates the oldest rock-hewn features at Lalibela to the 7th or 8th centuries, and scholars generally see four or five construction phases between the 7th and 13th centuries.
verdicts.note: Phillipson's 7th-8th century redating, about 500 years earlier than tradition, is set out in his World Archaeology feature; the Met independently states four or five phases between the 7th and 13th centuries.
